newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TRAINERS KNOW KEYS TO VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TRAINERS KNOW KEYS TO VICTORY.

text.p: Emanuel Steward, Lennox Lewis's trainer, knows the key to his fighter retaining the World Boxing Council heavyweight championship.
Don Turner, Henry Akinwande's trainer, knows the key to his fighter capturing the WBC heavyweight championship.
The question of which fighter will be able to lock up victory and the title will be settled on Saturday in a bout scheduled for 12 rounds.

"The whole key to this fight is who's going to take charge from the opening bell, and that's going to be Lennox," says Steward, who has trained or managed 27 world champions, including former four-time world champion Thomas Hearns and current WBC welterweight king Oscar De La Hoya.

"The key is for Henry to have his left jab and combination right going from the opening bell and make Lewis fight backing up," says Turner, who also trains World Boxing Association heavyweight champion Evander Holyfield.
Oddsmakers in Nevada seem to find Steward more convincing, rating Lewis an 8-to-5 favourite. The challenger, however, has been gaining support since Lewis was a 2-1 pick less than a week ago.
Refereeing the title clash will be Mills Lane, in his first bout since disqualifying Mike Tyson for biting Holyfield's ears two weeks ago.
This will be the sixth fight Steward has prepped Lewis, but he says it is the first time he's actually been happy with what the champion has displayed during training.
"I'm very happy, but for only the first time in more than two years of working with Lennox," says Steward. "That's because of the mental attitude Lennox has now.
"He's got a 'go out and take control' attitude now, instead of a 'go out and study and analyse an opponent for the first four rounds' attitude.
"Lennox was playing chess with his opponents, and I was sick and tired of it. But what we've been telling him, be more aggressive, has finally sunk in and he's taking full advantage of his talents."
Steward says Lewis, 31, found the right approach in the nick of time. "He needs to, because Akinwande is the most difficult fight of his career."
The fact that Akinwande is unbeaten, taller, has a longer reach and is quicker than Lewis, doesn't faze the champion.

"Akinwande has never been in with a guy like me," says Lewis, who at 6-foot-5 (1.96 m) and with an 84-inch (2.13 m) reach is anything but small himself. Still, he stands an inch and a half shorter (3.8 cm) and gives away two inches (5 cm) in reach.
"I'm stronger than the guys he's been in with. In this fight, my body shots should play a big part."
"Lennox said to me, 'I'm gonna knock him out'" says Steward. "He's never made a prediction like this before. That surprised me and pleased me both.
"Me, I don't expect it to go the distance, either, with Lennox winning by a late-round stoppage."
Neither Akinwande nor Turner are publically predicting a win by knockout, which makes sense since Lewis is regarded as the harder puncher of the two.
Akinwande has fashioned his record of 32-0-1, with 19 wins coming within the distance, thanks to a quick and sharp left jab followed by a solid, if not devastating, combination right.
"My strengths are movement and speed," says the 31-year-old Akinwande. "A lot of people say all I have is my jab, but I have other things. My strength is improving tremendously."
He will need to throw plenty of combinations in order to make Lewis back up.
The champion, who has a record of 30-1 with 25 wins ending early, has been unbeatable when advancing on an opponent, setting him up with stiff left jabs before launching powerful rights.
His lone loss came when Oliver McCall, a puncher, not a boxer, raced out at the opening bell, hurt Lewis in the first round and then finished him in the second of their September 1994 tilt.

That defeat dethroned Lewis, who had won the WBC title in 1993. Lewis regained the WBC crown in his most recent outing in February, when he dominated and stopped McCall, who quit fighting and appeared to suffer a psychological breakdown in the ring in the fifth round.
The ring size, 18 feet (5.5 m) square instead of the usual 20 feet (6 m), appears to favour Lewis in the championship bout at the 2,100-seat showroom of Caesars Tahoe.
